content:
I'm new to the Lean community, so nice to meet you all and I welcome any feedback!

I'm considering adding a feature to support alternative proofs. For example, I may have a theorem that is proven by clean_proof that is very clean and human readable AND it is also proven by fast_proof that is LLM-generated, less comprehensible, but faster to compile. Or I may have a proof that uses native decide and one that does not, but takes longer to compile.

What I am imagining is a system that has three proof alternatives: human readable (the reference proof; what is actually shown in the file; optimized for ease of understanding), fast (uses things like native decide, any shortcuts, perhaps we could even have an ultra-fast mode that uses heuristics), and thorough (avoids native decide, etc, maybe could even be extended for axiom-minimality).

The idea being that the ultimate source of truth may be a nightly thorough run, commits may use fast, while LSP/development may eventually support an ultra-fast heuristic mode. Another thought is we could throw LLMs at Mathlib to get type-checking time down, but we wouldn't want to lose the nice human proofs.

I'd love people's thoughts on this.

FYI, my background is using LLMs for Lean / Vericoding; some inspiration for this post is from zkPi.
In practice LLM generated proofs are almost always slower to compile though?

For something that is more about the pedagogical value of reproving the same thing there is the recall tactic, which allows you to restate/redefine/reprove the same thing up to defeq, and you can do so in a more literate way if you wish

E.g.

theorem my_theorem {a b c : Nat} : a + b + c = a + (b + c) := by grind

recall my_theorem {a b c : Nat} : a + b + c = a + (b + c) := by
  induction c with
  | zero =>
    show a + b + 0 = a + (b + 0)
    rfl
  | succ k ih =>
    show a + b + (k + 1) = a + (b + (k + 1))
    show (a + b + k) + 1 = a + (b + k) + 1
    guard_hyp ih :ₛ a + b + k = a + (b + k)
    exact congrArg (· + 1) ih

Zaz Brown said:

Another thought is we could throw LLMs at Mathlib to get type-checking time down, but we wouldn't want to lose the nice human proofs.

Technically, you can ask LLM to make file fasters and there is no doubt that advanced LLM is able to do so. In practice it is ridiculously expensive (as least for me I will not waste my token on it). You can physically look at the orange bar in the VScode to locate those slow checks, so (if you know how to fix the slow checks) asking your agent to do that is like spending $100 to tell you where the sun is in the sky, which is just physically shining over there. If you don't know how to fix them but just prompt "make it faster", some ridiculous fix could happen: spelling every simp onlyor speed up 1 file but slow down 10 downstream files.

Jeremy Chen said:

In practice LLM generated proofs are almost always slower to compile though?

I was thinking of using an LLM to optimize human proofs. I had a hunch that $500 worth of Astra Pro plan could half Mathlib compile time by finding all the annoying little compile-time optimizations that humans don't bother with and that make proofs messier. Or do you think there's not much room for optimization?

Jeremy Chen said:

For something that is more about the pedagogical value of reproving the same thing there is the recall tactic, which allows you to restate/redefine/reprove the same thing up to defeq, and you can do so in a more literate way if you wish

That's a really cool feature, but then Lean checks both definitions, right? Ideally, it would be good to add tags to recall, right?

So that, e.g. lake build checks the fastest proofs for each theorem, lake build --proofs pedagogical checks the recall(pedagogical) set of proofs, lake build --proofs all checks all of them. That kind of thing.

Because right now people are disincentivised from creating pedagogical recall proofs because it slows compile time, right?
@Jiaxi Mo Why would simp only slow down downstream files? It seems to me that, outside of rare cases, using an LLM along with benchmarking would usually make things better?

I don't think GPT could halve compile time. Maybe a percent or two really. And most of that comes from not golfing individual proofs, but more about the Lean toolchain itself. There's a cool graph here:
https://radar.lean-lang.org/repos/mathlib4/graph?m=build//instructions&zero=false&n=100000

Zaz Brown said:

Because right now people are disincentivised from creating pedagogical recall proofs because it slows compile time, right?

Not really. People don't use recall because writing a pedagogical exposition is not the intent of the work usually. Of course it doubles compile time, but a pedagogical proof is not really going to be any slower or faster to typecheck.

Zaz Brown said:

Jiaxi Mo Why would simp only slow down downstream files? It seems to me that, outside of rare cases, using an LLM along with benchmarking would usually make things better?

I think you combined the sentences together there; one point was about how an LLM reward hacking towards "compile time" might do the following: replace every simp with simp?, then commit to the suggestion, producing extremely long simp only [lemma1 ... lemma 30]s everywhere. While this may reduce compile time by a fraction, it creates very long and unreadable proofs. The other point was about reward hacking for "optimise Foo.lean" where it optimises Foo.lean at the cost of all other files, e.g. by deleting a theorem in Foo.lean and inlining it in all its use sites.
That is to say, there is no doubt you can use an LLM to help you optimise your proofs, just that you have to actually know what you are doing in most cases. Lean is a complicated language
